extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of American literature; literary critics and readers preparing author studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for reading, comparing, and judging early-20th-century American authors (poets, novelists, dramatists). Emphasizes what to notice, compare, and question when preparing critical readings or classroom assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sandburg — freedom from conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging Mr. Sandburg's work, it is important to remember that his theory involves complete freedom from conventions of all sorts--in thinking, in metrical form, and in vocabulary. His aim seems to be to reproduce the impressions that all phases of life make upon him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sandburg — consider prairie environment's effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether his early prairie environment had anything to do with the large scale of his imagination, the appeal to him of enormous periods of time, masses of men, and forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sandburg — universality in exaggerated localisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you find elements of universality in his exaggerated localisms? Do they combine to form a definite philosophy?

rubrics_metrics.name: Sandburg — effect of eccentricities and crudities of form
rubrics_metrics.description: What effect do the eccentricities and crudities of form have upon you? Do you consider them an essential part of his poetic expression or blemishes which he may one day overcome?

rubrics_metrics.name: Sandburg — weigh elements of greatness versus defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you find elements of greatness in Mr. Sandburg's work? Do you think they are likely to outweigh his obvious defects?

rubrics_metrics.name: Sandburg — compare democratic ideals with Lindsay
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare and contrast his democratic ideals with those of Lindsay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tarkington — separate study of boy-life and adolescence works
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider separately Mr. Tarkington's studies of boy life (especially Penrod), and of adolescence (especially Seventeen and Clarence). Judged by your own experience and observation, are they presented with true knowledge and humor, or are they a farcical skimming of surface eccentricities? Compare them with Mark Twain's books about boys and with Howells's Boy's Town.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tarkington — treat historical novels separately; is romance his field?
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider separately the historical novels. Is pure romance Mr. Tarkington's field? Why or why not?

rubrics_metrics.name: Tarkington — plot-completion as a test of artistic character
rubrics_metrics.description: According to all the codes of the more serious kinds of fiction, the unwillingness--or the inability--to conduct a plot to its legitimate ending implies some weakness in the artistic character; and this weakness is Mr. Tarkington's principal defect.... Now this causes the more regret for the reason that he has what is next best to character in a novelist--that is, knack. He has the knack of romance ... He has also the knack of satire, which he employs more frequently than romance ... he has traveled a long way from the methods of his greener days. Why, then, does he continue to trifle with his threadbare adolescents, as if he were afraid to write candidly about his coevals? Why does he drift with the sentimental tide and make propaganda for provincial complacency?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plot-completion and handling of adolescent material as focal points of criticism; weigh his 'knack' for romance and satire against the alleged plot weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tarkington — assess future direction and enduring value
rubrics_metrics.description: In what direction lies Mr. Tarkington's future? Is he likely to become more than a popular writer? What, if any, elements of enduring value do you find in his work?

rubrics_metrics.name: Tarkington — identify 'Hoosier' elements and compare regionally
rubrics_metrics.description: What 'Hoosier' elements do you find in his work? Compare him with Ade, Riley, Nicholson, and with the older writers of Indiana, Edward Eggleston, and Maurice Thompson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wharton — compare with Henry James using like material
rubrics_metrics.description: Mrs. Wharton's friendship with Henry James and the derivation of her methods from his suggest an interesting comparison of the work of these two writers. For this comparison, books treating of similar material should be chosen; for example, Mrs. Wharton's The Custom of the Country or Madame de Treymes with Mr. James's Portrait of a Lady or The Ambassadors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare method, treatment of similar subject matter, and how each author's mind shapes the inherited technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wharton — separate study of American social novels vs other works
rubrics_metrics.description: Mrs. Wharton's novels of American social life should be studied and judged separately from her Italian historical novel (The Valley of Decision) and from her New England stories, Ethan Frome and Summer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wharton — study supernatural effects and use of satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Two special phases of Mrs. Wharton's work which call for study are her management of supernatural effects in some of her short stories and her use of satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wharton — compare short stories with Mrs. Gerould
rubrics_metrics.description: Her short stories offer a basis of comparison with those of Mrs. Gerould, another disciple of Mr. James.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wharton — judge originality and claim to lasting distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Mrs. Wharton enough originality and enough distinction to hold a permanent high place as a novelist of American manners?

rubrics_metrics.name: Wharton — use Carl Van Doren criticisms as evaluative basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the following criticisms by Mr. Carl Van Doren as the basis of a critical judgment of your own: 'From the first Mrs. Wharton's power has lain in the ability to reproduce in fiction the circumstances of a compact community in a way that illustrates the various oppressions which such communities put upon individual vagaries... She has always been singularly unpartisan... It is only in these moments of satire that Mrs. Wharton reveals much about her disposition: her impatience of stupidity and affectation and muddy confusion of mind and purpose; her dislike of dinginess; her toleration of arrogance when it is high-bred.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Wharton's representation of compact communities, her alleged unpartisanship, and use of satire; decide whether Van Doren's characterization is fully correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wallace Stevens — study decorative/pictorial effects and formal experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Stevens's art is purely decorative, and its effects must be studied as in pictorial art. He is an experimenter in free verse forms as well as in impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on Stevens's visual/decorative effects, pictorial analogies, and his experiments in free verse and impressionistic techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sara Teasdale — simplicity, feeling, and perfection of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Sara Teasdale's love lyrics have been admired for their simplicity, feeling, and perfection of form. They need merely to be read to be appreciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating her lyrics emphasize clarity, emotional sincerity, and formal polish rather than experimental complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lew R. Sarett — authenticity in use of Indian material
rubrics_metrics.description: Many, Many Moons: A Book of Wilderness Poems is a reflection of his familiarity with Indian material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess his poems for accuracy, depth, and authenticity of Indian/wilderness representation; consider his background as woodsman and guide as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frederic Ridgely Torrence — study plays for a Negro theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Torrence's plays for a negro theatre are worth special study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give special critical attention to these plays as contributions to (African American) theatrical repertoire and consider their theatrical, cultural, and social contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horace Traubel — value as primary source for Whitman studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Traubel's account of his life there is of the greatest value for the study of Whitman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Traubel's diaries/biographical accounts as important primary-source material when studying Walt Whitman; assess reliability and unique firsthand insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edwin Meade Robinson — authenticity in boyhood portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Robinson has published a novel which has attracted attention as an honest record of a growing boy, Enter Jerry, 1920.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading Enter Jerry evaluate its authenticity and fidelity as a record of boyhood experience.
